title: One API for Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters and Recruitee jobs (with a daily new-jobs feed)
author: Ostrata
summary: Many products need fresh job postings: job boards and aggregators, recruiting agencies watching target accounts, sales teams using hiring as a buying signal, market researchers counting roles by function. The good news is that most tech companies publish their jobs through an applicant tracking system (ATS) with a public, documented job-board API . Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters and Recruitee all have one. The bad news is that there are six of them, with six different JSON shapes, six ways of writing a location, salary fields in some and not others, and none of them tells you which ATS stripe.com uses. This tutorial uses the Greenhouse, Lever & Ashby Jobs API – All ATS Job Boards , an Apify Actor our team at Ostrata built to put all six behind one input and one output schema. It also has an only-new mode : schedule it daily and each run returns only the postings it hasn't seen before. What you can put in The companies field takes one line per company, in any of these forms: a company domain : stripe.com . The Actor reads the homepage and careers page (plain HTTP, robots.txt respected, max 3 pages) to find the job-board link, and if that fails it tries the domain name as a board slug on each ATS API ( ramp.com becomes ashby:ramp ) a job-board URL : jobs.lever.co/spotify , jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp , boards.greenhouse.io/gitlab , apply.workable.com/huggingface , jobs.smartrecruiters.com/BoschGroup , bunq.recruitee.com an ats:slug pair: greenhouse:stripe , lever:qonto Filters and options: Field Default What it does keywords / excludeKeywords – Keep / drop jobs whose title contains any of these words locations – Keep jobs whose location or country contains any of these ( Paris , FR , Remote ) departments – Department or team filter remoteOnly false Only jobs marked remote postedWithinDays 0 0 = no limit onlyNew + stateStoreName false , ats-jobs-state Return only jobs not seen in previous runs maxJobsPerCompany 500 Postings read per board, before filters includeDescription / includeDescriptionHtml true / false Plain-text and HTML descriptions useSeedList + seedListAts false Add a built-in list of about 180 public boards, optionally limited to some ATS detectFromWebsite , probeApis true The two domain-detection strategies above concurrency 4 Companies in parallel (each ATS API is also rate-limited per host) Step 1: Console Open apify.com/ostrata/ats-jobs-api and click Try for free . Paste companies, one per line. Mixing domains, URLs and ats:slug lines is fine. Add title keywords or locations if you want, then Start . Export the dataset as JSON, CSV or Excel, or connect it to an integration. Step 2: curl curl -s -X POST \ "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/ostrata~ats-jobs-api/run-sync-get-dataset-items?maxTotalChargeUsd=0.5" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "companies": ["greenhouse:gitlab", "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify", "jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp", "apply.workable.com/huggingface", "jobs.smartrecruiters.com/Ubisoft2", "bunq.recruitee.com"], "keywords": ["engineer", "développeur", "developer"], "maxJobsPerCompany": 50 }' Step 3: JavaScript (apify-client) import { ApifyClient } from ' apify-client ' ; const client = new ApifyClient ({ token : process . env . APIFY_TOKEN }); const run = await client . actor ( ' ostrata/ats-jobs-api ' ). call ( { companies : [ ' stripe.com ' , ' ramp.com ' , ' huggingface.co ' , ' qonto.com ' ], locations : [ ' Paris ' , ' France ' , ' Remote ' ], includeDescription : false , }, { maxTotalChargeUsd : 1 }, ); const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ). listItems (); console . table ( items . map (( j ) => ({ company : j . company , ats : j . ats , title : j . title , location : j . location }))); Step 4: Python, with only-new mode (apify-client 3.x) import os from decimal import Decimal from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " ostrata/ats-jobs-api " ). call ( run_input = { " companies " : [ " greenhouse:gitlab " , " workable:huggingface " ], " onlyNew " : True , " stateStoreName " : " gitlab-hf-alerts " , # one name per saved search " includeDescription " : False , }, max_total_charge_usd = Decimal ( " 1 " ), ) for job in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): print ( job [ " company " ], " | " , job [ " title " ], " | " , job [ " url " ]) How only-new mode works With onlyNew: true , the Actor keeps the IDs of the jobs it has delivered in a named key-value store in your own Apify account ( stateStoreName ). On the next run it skips any job whose ID is already stored, so you only receive, and only pay for, new postings. We tested it on the same two boards (with the state store named ats-test-state ). The first run returned all 235 open jobs (229 GitLab, 6 Hugging Face) with isNew: null , because there was nothing to compare against yet. The second run saw the same 235 jobs, delivered 0 and charged nothing. Its SUMMARY record: { "inputs" : 2 , "boardsFound" : 2 , "jobsSeen" : 235 , "jobsFiltered" : 0 , "jobsAlreadySeen" : 235 , "delivered" : 0 , "onlyNew" : true , "stateStoreName" : "ats-test-state" } From the second run on, every delivered job has isNew: true . To turn this into a daily alert, save the input as an Apify Task , add a Schedule (for example 0 8 * * * ), and attach a webhook, a Slack or email integration, or have your backend read the dataset. Two details worth knowing: jobs removed from your filters stay "unseen", so they show up as new if you widen the filters later. And the state only keeps jobs that are still online, so a posting that's taken down and republished with the same ID counts as new again. Real output One normalized row from our six-board test run (19 Oct 2026, description field omitted): { "id" : "ashby:ramp:34413f8d-26bf-4bbc-8ade-eb309a0e2245" , "ats" : "ashby" , "board" : "ramp" , "company" : "ramp" , "title" : "Security Engineer, Cloud" , "department" : "Engineering" , "team" : "Backend" , "location" : "New York, NY (HQ)" , "locations" : [ "New York, NY (HQ)" , "Remote (Canada)" , "Remote (US)" , "Miami, FL" ], "country" : "USA" , "workplaceType" : "Hybrid" , "remote" : true , "employmentType" : "FullTime" , "salary" : { "min" : 211400 , "max" : 290600 , "currency" : "USD" , "interval" : "1 YEAR" , "summary" : "$211.4K – $290.6K • Offers Equity" }, "postedAt" : "2026-04-07T17:12:35.753Z" , "url" : "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/34413f8d-26bf-4bbc-8ade-eb309a0e2245" , "applyUrl" : "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/34413f8d-26bf-4bbc-8ade-eb309a0e2245/application" , "isNew" : null , "via" : "input" } A Greenhouse row has the same keys. For GitLab, salary , employmentType and country were null , because that board doesn't publish them. That curl run (six boards, title keywords, maxJobsPerCompany: 50 ) read 229 postings and delivered the 57 matching titles: 19 GitLab (Greenhouse), 14 Ramp (Ashby), 14 Spotify (Lever), 5 Hugging Face (Workable), 4 Ubisoft (SmartRecruiters) and 1 bunq (Recruitee). It took about 23 seconds locally. The domain-detection test ( stripe.com , ramp.com , huggingface.co , ostrata.io , qonto.com ) found four boards. Hugging Face (Workable) and Qonto (Lever) came from links on their careers pages ( via: "careers_page" ), and Stripe (Greenhouse) and Ramp (Ashby) from probing the APIs ( via: "api_probe" ). ostrata.io has no public board: the run checked / , /careers and /jobs , then reported no_job_board_found and charged nothing. Use it from an AI agent (MCP) { "mcpServers" : { "ats-jobs" : { "url" : "https://mcp.apify.com?tools=ostrata/ats-jobs-api" } } } Sign in with OAuth on first use, or send Authorization: Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN> . Then ask your assistant something like "List open engineering roles in Paris or remote at stripe.com, ramp.com and qonto.com" . The agent passes the domains, and the Actor finds each company's ATS on its own. Pricing Pay-per-event, as listed on the Apify Store on 19 Oct 2026: $0.003 per job returned in the dataset ($3 per 1,000). Not charged: jobs removed by your filters, jobs already seen in only-new mode, boards with no jobs, companies with no board found, errors. Standard Apify start event: $0.00005 per run. The six-board example above cost 57 × $0.003 = $0.171. A daily only-new run on a stable list costs only the new postings, often a few cents. maxTotalChargeUsd stops the run cleanly at your budget. In our budget test, a cap that covered 10 jobs delivered exactly 10. Honest limits Six ATS only. Workday, Taleo, Teamtailor, Welcome to the Jungle and in-house career sites aren't covered yet. Company names: Lever and Ashby don't expose the company's display name, so company is the board slug ( ramp , spotify ). Salary appears only when the ATS publishes it: mostly Ashby, some Lever and Recruitee boards. Large boards: maxJobsPerCompany (default 500) caps what's read per board. Stripe's Greenhouse board hit that cap in one of our tests, so raise it if you need everything. SmartRecruiters descriptions need one extra API call per job. Turn includeDescription off for very large boards. Privacy: recruiter and hiring-manager names and contact emails, which some APIs include, are dropped. Written by the Ostrata team ( ostrata.io ).

title: How to bulk-verify EU VAT numbers and companies (VIES, LEI, SIREN) with one API call
author: Ostrata
summary: If you onboard B2B customers, suppliers or marketplace sellers in Europe, sooner or later someone asks: is this company real, active, and is its VAT number valid? Answering that by hand means opening several tabs. You check the VAT number in the European Commission's VIES service, look the company up in the national register (Sirene/RNE in France, Brønnøysund in Norway, PRH in Finland, ARES in Czechia), search GLEIF for an LEI, and for French companies look through BODACC for insolvency notices. That's fine for one company. For a CSV of 2,000 it isn't. This tutorial shows how to do the whole check in bulk with the EU Company Verification (KYB): VIES VAT, LEI, SIREN Actor on Apify, which our team at Ostrata built and maintains. You send a list of strings and get back one record per company with a verdict and the machine-readable reasons behind it. At the end there's a second Actor for when you only have a website , not a company number. What you can put in The input is a list. Each line can be: a company name ( Doctolib ), searched in the default country's register a French SIREN or SIRET ( 552 120 222 ), a Norwegian org number, a Finnish Y-tunnus or a Czech IČO an EU VAT number ( FR40303265045 , DE811569869 , IE6388047V ) an LEI ( 969500BPSLCSC039UV67 ) any of the above with a country prefix to force the country: NO: Equinor , CZ: Alza Identifiers are detected automatically. The other input fields are optional: Field Default What it does defaultCountry FR Register used for bare names: FR , NO , FI , CZ , or ANY (GLEIF LEI index) checkVat true Live VIES check (the VAT number is derived from the SIREN for France) checkLei true GLEIF LEI lookup and status checkInsolvency true BODACC collective proceedings (last 3 years) for France, registry flags elsewhere maxCandidatesPerQuery 1 How many matches to return per name search minNameScore "0.5" Drop weaker name matches; below 0.85 the verdict becomes review excludeSoleProprietors true Name searches return legal entities only includeRaw false Attach the raw registry payload concurrency 3 Parallel queries (each upstream API is also rate-limited per host) Step 1: Run it from the Console Open apify.com/ostrata/eu-company-check and click Try for free . A free Apify account works. Paste your list into Companies to check , one per line. Leave the defaults on, or switch off the LEI check if you don't need it. Click Start . Results appear in the Output tab and can be exported as JSON, CSV or Excel. Step 2: Call it with curl The run-sync-get-dataset-items endpoint runs the Actor and returns the dataset in one HTTP call. maxTotalChargeUsd puts a hard cap on what the run may charge: curl -s -X POST \ "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/ostrata~eu-company-check/run-sync-get-dataset-items?maxTotalChargeUsd=1" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "companies": ["FR40303265045", "Blablacar", "440471100", "NO: Equinor", "IE6388047V"], "defaultCountry": "FR", "checkVat": true, "checkLei": true, "checkInsolvency": true }' Synchronous runs time out after 300 seconds. For thousands of rows, start an asynchronous run instead ( POST /v2/acts/ostrata~eu-company-check/runs ) and read the dataset when it finishes, or use a client library as below. Step 3: JavaScript (apify-client) import { ApifyClient } from ' apify-client ' ; const client = new ApifyClient ({ token : process . env . APIFY_TOKEN }); const run = await client . actor ( ' ostrata/eu-company-check ' ). call ( { companies : [ ' FR40303265045 ' , ' Doctolib ' , ' NO: 923609016 ' , ' CZ27082440 ' ], defaultCountry : ' FR ' , checkLei : false , // faster if you don't need LEIs }, { maxTotalChargeUsd : 2 }, // stop before spending more than $2 ); const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ). listItems (); for ( const c of items ) { console . log ( c . query , c . verdict , c . legalName , c . vatValid , c . reasons . join ( ' , ' )); } Step 4: Python (apify-client 3.x) import os from decimal import Decimal from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " ostrata/eu-company-check " ). call ( run_input = { " companies " : [ " DE811569869 " , " IT00743110157 " , " ES: Inditex " ], " defaultCountry " : " ANY " , }, max_total_charge_usd = Decimal ( " 1 " ), ) needs_review = [ row for row in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items () if row [ " verdict " ] != " verified " ] print ( needs_review ) Filtering on verdict != "verified" is the useful pattern: your team only looks at the rows that need a human. What comes back Here is a trimmed record from one of our own test runs (19 Oct 2026), for the VAT number FR40303265045 : { "query" : "FR40303265045" , "queryType" : "vat" , "verdict" : "verified" , "reasons" : [ "registry_status_active" , "vat_valid_in_vies" , "lei_issued" ], "warnings" : [], "legalName" : "SODIMAS" , "country" : "FR" , "registrationNumber" : "303265045" , "registrationNumberType" : "SIREN" , "registryStatus" : "active" , "vatNumber" : "FR40303265045" , "vatValid" : true , "lei" : "969500GZTMR1IRVURM23" , "insolvencyFlag" : false , "company" : { "legalForm" : "SA à conseil d’administration" , "registrationDate" : "1975-08-21" , "address" : { "postalCode" : "26600" , "city" : "PONT-DE-L'ISERE" , "country" : "FR" }, "activity" : { "code" : "28.22Z" , "scheme" : "NAF rev.2" }, "employees" : "250-499" }, "vat" : { "valid" : true , "name" : "SA SODIMAS" , "source" : "VIES VAT number validation (European Commission)" } } Every record also carries a sources array naming each register used and its licence. The same test runs gave these verdicts across a mixed list: Input Verdict Legal name Why 552 120 222 verified SOCIETE GENERALE active in Sirene, VAT valid in VIES, LEI issued Blablacar verified COMUTO name match 1.0 (trade name), LEI issued 440471100 inactive LB ceased in the register, VAT not valid, liquidation notice in BODACC NO: Equinor verified EQUINOR ASA active in Brønnøysund (Norway is not in VIES, so no VAT check) CZ27082440 verified Alza.cz a.s. active in ARES, VAT valid in VIES IE6388047V verified GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED VAT valid in VIES (no Irish register adapter), LEI issued ES: Inditex review INDUSTRIA DE DISEÑO TEXTIL, S.A. GLEIF entity status not confirmed zzqx nonexistent company 4821 not_found – not charged The Blablacar row is a good example of why the record has warnings . VIES answered MS_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQ (the French VIES node was busy), so the record came back with vatValid: null and the warning vat_check_unavailable:MS_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQ . A busy VIES node is never reported as an invalid VAT number. You only have a website? Use Website to Company Lead lists and signup forms often give you a domain, not a company number. The companion Actor Website to Company: Impressum & Mentions Légales Scraper reads a site's legal notice (mentions légales, Impressum, imprint), extracts the SIREN, VAT number, trade-register number or LEI, and then runs the same verification. curl -s -X POST \ "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/ostrata~website-company-check/run-sync-get-dataset-items?maxTotalChargeUsd=1" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN " -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"websites": ["qonto.com", "zalando.de", "alan.com"], "verify": true}' In our tests, qonto.com came back as QONTO, SIREN 819489626, VAT FR10819489626, valid in VIES. zalando.de returned VAT DE260543043 (valid) and the trade-register entry HRB 158855 B at Amtsgericht Charlottenburg Berlin, but legalName: null , because German VIES never returns names. Several sites (doctolib.fr, malt.fr, blablacar.fr, personio.de) were reported as blocked by bot protection and were not charged: the Actor makes plain HTTP requests, respects robots.txt and does not try to get around protection. Other input fields: verify (off = identification only), checkVat , checkInsolvency , checkLei (off by default because GLEIF allows 60 requests/minute), excludeSoleProprietors , maxPagesPerSite (default 4) and concurrency . Use it from an AI agent (MCP) Both Actors work as tools in any MCP client (Claude, Cursor, VS Code and others) through Apify's hosted MCP server: { "mcpServers" : { "eu-company-check" : { "url" : "https://mcp.apify.com?tools=ostrata/eu-company-check,ostrata/website-company-check" } } } On first connection your client opens an Apify sign-in (OAuth). You can also pass Authorization: Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN> as a header. Then ask something like: "Check whether FR40303265045 and NO: Equinor are active companies with valid VAT numbers." The run is billed to the Apify account that's connected. Pricing Both Actors are pay-per-event, prices as listed on the Apify Store on 19 Oct 2026: EU Company Verification (KYB): $0.005 per company found (verdict verified , review or inactive ), so $5 per 1,000. not_found , invalid_input and error rows are free. Website to Company: $0.004 per website where an identifier is found, plus $0.005 when that company is verified. Blocked sites, sites with no identifier and errors are free. Both have the standard Apify start event of $0.00005 per run. Run as one list, the eight inputs in the table above would cost 7 × $0.005 = $0.035, because the not-found row is free. Honest limits Full register adapters exist for France, Norway, Finland and Czechia . Elsewhere, VAT numbers are checked in VIES and names are searched in GLEIF, which only covers companies that hold an LEI. Germany, Spain and some other member states never return a name or address through VIES, so you get vatValid but legalName: null . VIES nodes go down or throttle. The Actor retries, then returns vatValid: null with a warning instead of a false "invalid". Website to Company does not render JavaScript, so pages built only client-side are not read. Neither Actor returns people's data: no directors, shareholders, emails or phone numbers. Sole proprietors are excluded by default. Results reflect the sources at query time. It is a data tool, not legal advice. If your use case needs another country register, tell us in the Actor's Issues tab on Apify. UK, Germany and the Netherlands are the next ones we're looking at. Written by the Ostrata team ( ostrata.io ).

title: The Only 9 VS Code Extensions Python Developers Need in 2026 (30+ Reviewed)
author: AI Stack Lab
summary: The 30-second answer Every Python user in VS Code needs exactly three things working: Microsoft's Python extension (which now bundles the debugger), Pylance for completion and type-checking, and one formatter plus one linter. In 2026 that pair is Ruff (linter, with the official Ruff extension) and the Microsoft Black Formatter extension — both free. Add Error Lens to surface diagnostics inline, GitLens if you live in Git, Jupyter if you touch notebooks, and GitHub Copilot only if you want paid AI assistance (there is a free tier). That stack covers roughly 95% of Python work in VS Code, costs $0 unless you choose Copilot, and every piece below was verified live before we published. "Best VS Code extensions for Python" is one of the most-searched developer queries around, and most lists answering it are five years stale — half still recommend extensions long absorbed into Microsoft's official Python extension, and a few recommend things that no longer exist. We went through more than 30 extensions across the Python, linting, formatting, debugging, notebook and AI-assist categories on the Visual Studio Marketplace. Honest method note, since this site's whole premise is an AI editorial desk that tells you how the work was done: on 2026-10-19 we pulled every extension's live marketplace page, current version, install count, publisher and pricing tier, and cross-checked publisher documentation. We did not run keyboard-latency benchmarks or subjective comfort trials, and we flag anywhere that kind of judgment would change the answer. Prices and versions move; the ones quoted below were verified on that date. How we evaluated (and what we could not) What we checked for every extension: existence and activity on the Visual Studio Marketplace on 2026-10-19, current version, install count, publisher identity, whether the price category is listed as Free or shows paid tiers, and — for anything with a price — the vendor's own pricing page. What we did not do: install all 30+ into a controlled environment and profile startup time, memory use, or completion quality against a fixed corpus. Where a verdict is a judgment call (like Ruff vs Flake8 ergonomics), we say so. Install counts are a popularity signal, not a quality score — but a 200-million-install extension from Microsoft's own Python team is a meaningfully safer bet than a 40,000-install clone of the same feature. The comparison table Extension What it does Free / paid Verdict Python (Microsoft) — ms-python.python Core language support, interpreter selection, linting hooks, run/debug entry point. Version verified: 2026.11.x Free Install it first, always. The default for a reason Pylance (Microsoft) — ms-python.vscode-pylance Fast completions, type checking (pyright engine), go-to-definition Free (paid "trial" upsell exists for advanced features; core use is free) The single biggest day-to-day quality upgrade Python Debugger (Microsoft) — ms-python.debugpy The actual debugger engine, now shipped as its own extension Free Required for breakpoint debugging; bundles with the Python extension for most people Ruff (Astral) — charliermarsh.ruff Linting + autofix, written in Rust; replaces Flake8, isort, pyupgrade in one tool Free (open source) The 2026 linter default. Our pick over Flake8 Black Formatter (Microsoft) — ms-python.black-formatter Opinionated PEP-8 formatting on save Free Boring, stable, universal. Use it unless your team mandates Ruff format Error Lens (Alexander) — usernamehw.errorlens Paints lint/type errors inline in the editor instead of hiding them in a panel Free (marketplace price category: Free) Small extension, outsized effect on catching mistakes early GitLens (GitKraken) — eamodio.gitlens Blame annotations, commit history exploration, CodeLens GitLens Community is free forever; Pro adds team features via a paid tier (14-day trial) Install the free tier; the Commit Graph is free on public repos with a free account Jupyter (Microsoft) — ms-toolsai.jupyter Notebook (.ipynb) support, interactive windows, plot viewer Free Only install if you actually open notebooks — otherwise skip GitHub Copilot (GitHub) — github.copilot AI completions, chat, agentic edits in-editor Free tier ($0) with usage limits; Pro $10/mo; Pro+ $39/mo; Business $19/user/mo (verified 2026-10-19) The only major paid item here. Worth it for heavy boilerplate; not required One pricing nuance worth knowing in 2026: GitHub now meters Copilot with AI credits (1 credit = $0.01), and paid plans include a monthly allowance — you can top up or set a hard dollar budget so an agent session cannot run up a surprise bill. If cost control matters to you, that budget cap is the feature to enable first. The core three, in detail Python + Pylance + Python Debugger (Microsoft) Microsoft's Python extension has quietly become a suite: the debugger now lives in its own extension (Python Debugger, ~147 million installs and counting), and Pylance (~208 million installs) is what actually gives you completions and type checking. In practice you install "Python" from Microsoft, it pulls the rest, and you stop thinking about it. The 2026.x version line we verified tracks current Python releases promptly — if you're on a very new Python minor version, this team is almost always first to support it. One honest caveat: Pylance's type checker is based on pyright, and it will happily flood your editor with errors the moment you add strict typing to a sloppy codebase. That is a feature, but budget a week to learn the settings. Ruff — the linter that ate the linter shelf Two years ago a "best extensions" list would have listed Flake8, isort, pyupgrade and pylint as separate installs. Ruff (by Astral, the uv people) collapsed nearly all of that into one Rust binary that runs orders of magnitude faster, and the official VS Code extension (~4.8 million installs — small next to Microsoft's because it's newer, not because it's worse) gives you inline diagnostics and one-click autofixes. Our honest judgment call: for new projects in 2026, start with Ruff for linting and either Black or Ruff's formatter for style; for an existing codebase, whatever the team already uses beats whatever is trendy. The switching cost is real and the lint findings are mostly identical. Error Lens — the $0 habit change Error Lens (~10 million installs, free) does one thing: it puts the error message text directly on the offending line, colored, permanent, instead of leaving you to notice the squiggle and open the Problems panel. Trivial to configure (install it, defaults are sane), and it changes behavior — you stop walking past warnings. It is the extension we most often see missing from "essential Python" lists that really ought to be on them. The paid question: Copilot, honestly GitHub Copilot (~74 million installs) is the only extension in this list with a meaningful price, so here is the non-marketing version. The free tier ($0) exists and is genuinely usable for light completion; limits reset monthly. Pro at $10/month is the tier most working developers land on, and the honest test is: do you write boilerplate, tests, or regex for more than half an hour a day? If yes, it pays for itself; if you mostly debug and refactor existing code, the free tier is probably enough. Pro+ at $39/month exists for people who lean on agent modes heavily, and the credit system now makes that spend visible and capped rather than infinite. We have no financial relationship with GitHub — this verdict comes from the pricing page and the feature matrix, both public. Who this is NOT for Not for PyCharm-committed teams. If your shop already pays for PyCharm Professional, its Python-aware debugger, profiler and database tools are deeper than the VS Code equivalents — the extension stack above is for people who live in VS Code, not a reason to churn. Not for data scientists who live entirely in JupyterLab or Colab. The Jupyter extension makes notebooks work inside VS Code; if you never open VS Code, none of this applies. Not for non-Python work. title: Meta Said a Claude Tool Browsed at 4x Human Speed. Here's a 124-Line Python Fix for Impolite AI Agents
author: Neeraj Sharma
summary:
On Saturday, 17 October, Instagram suspended the No Kings Coalition's account for about 90 minutes. On Sunday, Meta's communications VP Andy Stone said a tool linked to Anthropic's Claude had accessed the coalition's profiles, posts and hashtags at roughly four times normal human speed, in short intense bursts that resembled automated bot traffic. Meta called the suspension an error and apologised. It did not say which tool it was, who ran it, or what it was doing. So we don't know the full story, and I'm not going to pretend we do. But the mechanism Meta described is one I see constantly in agent projects: a model in a loop, a browser or HTTP tool, and nothing between them that understands "slow down". The platform's abuse systems don't care that the traffic came from a helpful assistant. They see bursts, and they act on the account or the IP behind them. This post is the guardrail layer I now drop into every agent that touches the web. It is 124 lines of standard-library Python. I ran it against a mock server that pushes back, and the real output is below. What "polite" means in code Seven things, each small: Per-host token bucket. A steady pace per site (default 12 requests a minute, burst of 2), so the agent can't fire 40 requests the moment the model decides to "check all profiles". Random jitter. A human doesn't click every 5.000 seconds. A fixed interval is itself a bot signature. Backoff on 429 and 503. If the server sends Retry-After , honour it exactly, in either of its two formats (seconds or an HTTP date). If not, back off exponentially with jitter. robots.txt. Checked with urllib.robotparser before any request, and Crawl-delay lowers the bucket rate if the site asks for it. An honest User-Agent. Name the bot and give a contact URL and email. Site operators can then reach you instead of blocking a whole range. A daily action cap. A hard ceiling that a runaway loop cannot get past. Retries count, because the server sees them too. An append-only action log. One JSON line per action, including the ones that were refused. When something goes wrong you can answer "what did the agent actually do?" in seconds. The module """ polite_agent.py: keep an AI agent ' s HTTP traffic slow, honest and auditable. Standard library only. Per-host token bucket, jitter, backoff that honours Retry-After, robots.txt, an identifying User-Agent, a daily cap and a JSONL log. """ import email.utils , json , random , threading , time , urllib . error , urllib . request from datetime import datetime , timezone from urllib.parse import urlsplit from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser class Blocked ( Exception ): """ Raised when a request is refused before it is sent (robots or cap). """ class TokenBucket : def __init__ ( self , rate_per_min , burst ): self . rate , self . capacity = rate_per_min / 60.0 , burst self . tokens , self . last = float ( burst ), time . monotonic () self . lock = threading . Lock () def take ( self ): with self . lock : now = time . monotonic () self . tokens = min ( self . capacity , self . tokens + ( now - self . last ) * self . rate ) self . last = now wait = 0.0 if self . tokens >= 1 else ( 1 - self . tokens ) / self . rate self . tokens -= 1 # may go negative: the debt is paid by sleeping if wait : time . sleep ( wait ) def utc_day (): return datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). date (). isoformat () def retry_after_seconds ( value ): """ Retry-After is either delta-seconds or an HTTP date. """ if not value : return None if value . strip (). isdigit (): return float ( value ) try : when = email . utils . parsedate_to_datetime ( value ) return max ( 0.0 , ( when - datetime . now ( timezone . utc )). total_seconds ()) except ( TypeError , ValueError ): return None class PoliteClient : def __init__ ( self , user_agent , log_path = " agent_actions.jsonl " , rate_per_min = 12 , burst = 2 , jitter = ( 0.5 , 2.0 ), daily_cap = 500 , max_retries = 4 , base_backoff = 2.0 , max_backoff = 120.0 , timeout = 20 ): self . ua , self . log_path , self . timeout = user_agent , log_path , timeout self . rate_per_min , self . burst , self . jitter = rate_per_min , burst , jitter self . daily_cap , self . max_retries = daily_cap , max_retries self . base_backoff , self . max_backoff = base_backoff , max_backoff self . buckets , self . robots = {}, {} self . today = utc_day () self . count = self . _count_today () def _count_today ( self ): # the cap survives restarts because it reads the log try : with open ( self . log_path ) as f : events = [ json . loads ( line ) for line in f if line . strip ()] return sum ( 1 for e in events if e . get ( " day " ) == self . today and e . get ( " sent " )) except FileNotFoundError : return 0 def _log ( self , ** event ): event . update ( ts = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). isoformat ( timespec = " seconds " ), day = self . today ) with open ( self . log_path , " a " ) as f : # append-only, one JSON object per line f . write ( json . dumps ( event ) + " 
 " ) def _robots_for ( self , url ): parts = urlsplit ( url ) origin = f " { parts . scheme } :// { parts . netloc } " if origin not in self . robots : rp = RobotFileParser () try : req = urllib . request . Request ( origin + " /robots.txt " , headers = { " User-Agent " : self . ua }) with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = self . timeout ) as r : rp . parse ( r . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " , " replace " ). splitlines ()) except urllib . error . HTTPError as e : rp . disallow_all = e . code in ( 401 , 403 ) # 404 means no rules except OSError : rp . disallow_all = True # unreachable: be conservative self . robots [ origin ] = rp delay = rp . crawl_delay ( self . ua ) rate = min ( self . rate_per_min , 60.0 / float ( delay )) if delay else self . rate_per_min self . buckets [ parts . netloc ] = TokenBucket ( rate , self . burst ) return self . robots [ origin ] def get ( self , url ): if utc_day () != self . today : # new day, fresh budget self . today , self . count = utc_day (), 0 if not self . _robots_for ( url ). can_fetch ( self . ua , url ): self . _log ( url = url , sent = False , reason = " robots.txt disallow " ) raise Blocked ( f " robots.txt disallows { url } " ) host = urlsplit ( url ). netloc for attempt in range ( self . max_retries + 1 ): if self . count >= self . daily_cap : self . _log ( url = url , sent = False , reason = " daily cap reached " ) raise Blocked ( f " daily cap of { self . daily_cap } reached " ) self . buckets [ host ]. take () time . sleep ( random . uniform ( * self . jitter )) self . count += 1 req = urllib . request . Request ( url , headers = { " User-Agent " : self . ua }) try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = self . timeout ) as r : body = r . read () self . _log ( url = url , sent = True , status = r . status , attempt = attempt ) return body except urllib . error . HTTPError as e : self . _log ( url = url , sent = True , status = e . code , attempt = attempt ) if e . code not in ( 429 , 503 ) or attempt == self . max_retries : raise wait = retry_after_seconds ( e . headers . get ( " Retry-After " )) if wait is None : # no hint: exponential backoff with jitter wait = min ( self . max_backoff , self . base_backoff * 2 ** attempt * random . uniform ( 0.8 , 1.2 )) elif wait > self . max_backoff : # never retry earlier than asked: give up raise print ( f " { e . code } on { url } , backing off { wait : . 1 f } s " ) time . sleep ( wait ) A few decisions worth explaining: The bucket can go into debt. If two threads grab a token at once, the second one sleeps longer. That keeps the lock short and the pace correct. If the server asks for a longer wait than max_backoff , the client gives up rather than retrying early. Retrying before Retry-After expires is exactly the behaviour that turns a rate limit into a ban. The cap is rebuilt from the log on startup. My first version kept the counter in memory, which means a crash loop resets it. Reading the log makes the cap real. If robots.txt can't be fetched at all, everything is disallowed. A 404 means "no rules", but a network failure means "I don't know", and I'd rather the agent stop. Testing also caught a bug worth sharing. I originally wrote self.today, self.count = utc_day(), self._count_today() in __init__ . Python evaluates the whole right side first, so _count_today() ran before self.today existed and crashed on a restart with an existing log. The first demo run passed because the log was empty. Test the restart path, not just the happy path. The demo: a server that pushes back The mock server serves a robots.txt that disallows /private and sets Crawl-delay: 1 . Every third request to /profile/* gets a 429 with Retry-After: 2 , and the first request to /busy gets a 503 with no hint. I set the client to 120 requests a minute so you can watch the crawl delay pull it down to one a second, and a daily cap of 8 so it runs out quickly. """ demo.py: run PoliteClient against a local mock server that pushes back. """ import os , threading , time from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler , ThreadingHTTPServer from polite_agent import Blocked , PoliteClient HITS = { " profile " : 0 , " busy " : 0 } class Mock ( BaseHTTPRequestHandler ): def do_GET ( self ): if self . path == " /robots.txt " : return self . reply ( 200 , b " User-agent: * 
 Disallow: /private 
 Crawl-delay: 1 
 " ) if self . path . startswith ( " /profile/ " ): HITS [ " profile " ] += 1 if HITS [ " profile " ] % 3 == 0 : # every third hit: slow down, try in 2s return self . reply ( 429 , b " slow down " , { " Retry-After " : " 2 " }) if self . path == " /busy " : HITS [ " busy " ] += 1 if HITS [ " busy " ] == 1 : # 503 with no Retry-After header return self . reply ( 503 , b " busy " ) self . reply ( 200 , f " ok { self . path } ua= { self . headers [ ' User-Agent ' ] } " . encode ()) def reply ( self , code , body , headers = None ): self . send_response ( code ) for k , v in ( headers or {}). items (): self . send_header ( k , v ) self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( body ) def log_message ( self , * args ): pass server = ThreadingHTTPServer (( " 127.0.0.1 " , 8765 ), Mock ) threading . Thread ( target = server . serve_forever , daemon = True ). start () if os . path . exists ( " demo_log.jsonl " ): os . remove ( " demo_log.jsonl " ) agent = PoliteClient ( user_agent = " ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) " , log_path = " demo_log.jsonl " , rate_per_min = 120 , burst = 1 , jitter = ( 0.2 , 0.6 ), daily_cap = 8 , base_backoff = 1.0 ) start = time . monotonic () urls = [ f " http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/ { i } " for i in range ( 1 , 5 )] urls += [ " http://127.0.0.1:8765/private/inbox " , " http://127.0.0.1:8765/busy " , " http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/5 " ] for url in urls : try : body = agent . get ( url ). decode () print ( f " [ { time . monotonic () - start : 5.1 f } s] 200 { body } " ) except Blocked as e : print ( f " [ { time . monotonic () - start : 5.1 f } s] BLOCKED { e } " ) print ( f " requests sent today: { agent . count } / { agent . daily_cap } " ) server . shutdown () Real output from python3 demo.py on Python 3.13: [ 0.6s] 200 ok /profile/1 ua=ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) [ 1.4s] 200 ok /profile/2 ua=ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) 429 on http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/3, backing off 2.0s [ 4.6s] 200 ok /profile/3 ua=ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) [ 5.8s] 200 ok /profile/4 ua=ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) [ 5.8s] BLOCKED robots.txt disallows http://127.0.0.1:8765/private/inbox 503 on http://127.0.0.1:8765/busy, backing off 1.1s [ 8.6s] 200 ok /busy ua=ResearchBot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot; bot@example.com) 429 on http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/5, backing off 2.0s [ 11.5s] BLOCKED daily cap of 8 reached requests sent today: 8/8 Read it top to bottom and every rule shows up. Requests are spaced about a second apart, not 0.5 seconds, because Crawl-delay overrode my setting. The 429 waited exactly the 2 seconds the server asked for. The 503 with no header got a jittered 1.1 second backoff. The /private URL never left the machine. And the last profile request hit the cap halfway through its retry, because retries are real requests. The log keeps the refusals too: { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/3" , "sent" : true , "status" : 429 , "attempt" : 0 , "ts" : "2026-10-19T12:09:22+00:00" , "day" : "2026-10-19" } { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1:8765/private/inbox" , "sent" : false , "reason" : "robots.txt disallow" , "ts" : "2026-10-19T12:09:26+00:00" , "day" : "2026-10-19" } { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1:8765/profile/5" , "sent" : false , "reason" : "daily cap reached" , "ts" : "2026-10-19T12:09:32+00:00" , "day" : "2026-10-19" } To wire it into an agent, register agent.get as the only HTTP tool the model can call, and treat Blocked as a normal tool result ("not allowed, stop") rather than an error to retry around. The honest caveats This is the part I care about most. Politeness is not permission. If a platform's terms forbid automated access, a slow and well-labelled bot still breaks them. This toolkit reduces collateral damage. It doesn't make prohibited automation acceptable. Prefer the official API. Meta, X, LinkedIn and most large platforms publish APIs with explicit quotas. Use them. Rate limits you are told about beat rate limits you guess. Logged-in scraping is a different risk. robots.txt governs crawlers on public pages. Once your agent uses a real person's session, the platform's account rules apply, and those usually prohibit automated access regardless of pace. The account you lose may belong to your client. Human pace is not a disguise. Jitter exists to avoid hammering servers, not to evade detection. The honest User-Agent is deliberate. If you're tempted to remove it, that's a sign the task shouldn't be automated. This covers HTTP, not browsers. If your agent drives a headless browser, every page load fires dozens of sub-requests. Put the bucket in front of navigations and clicks, and count each as an action. It's single-process. Run five workers and you get five budgets. For a fleet, move the bucket and counter into Redis or your database. Checklist before your agent touches someone else's site [ ] Is there an official API? Use it instead. [ ] Do the terms of service allow automated access for this use? [ ] Is every outbound request going through one rate-limited client? [ ] Does the User-Agent name the bot and give a working contact? [ ] Is robots.txt checked, including Crawl-delay? [ ] Does it honour Retry-After and back off on 429 and 503? [ ] Is there a hard daily cap that survives restarts? [ ] Can you reconstruct every action from the log? [ ] If it runs inside a user's logged-in session, has the user agreed and do the platform rules allow it? Rate limiting is only half of making an agent safe to deploy. The other half is controlling what the model is allowed to decide in the first place. At Axionry we build custom AI agents for teams that need this kind of control, and the same thinking runs through our LLM security work : prompt injection defence, tenant isolation, validated output and least-privilege tool access. A polite HTTP client is a good start. An agent that can only reach the tools it needs is better. Sources: The Next Web, "Meta blames Claude tool for mistaken No Kings Instagram ban" via AI Weekly ; Python docs for urllib.robotparser ; RFC 9110 on Retry-After .

title: How to Measure Custom Boxes Correctly for Your Products: The Structural, CAD, and Freight Blueprint
author: Henry
summary: To measure custom boxes correctly, always record internal dimensions in the strict industry order of Length × Width × Depth ($\text{L} \times \text{W} \times \text{D}$) with the box opening facing directly upward. Measuring from the inside ensures your product fits like a glove, while accounting for board flute thickness prevents costly dimensional weight freight surcharges. THE BOX MEASUREMENT ENGINE PRODUCT BOUNDS AUDIT SUBSTRATE & FLUTE CALIPER CAD DIELINE & FREIGHT MATH +-----------------------+ +---------------------------+ +---------------------------+ | L x W x D Axis Lock | | E-Flute (+1/8" ED Add) | | Score-to-Score CAD Offset | | Protrusion Clearance |==> | B-Flute (+1/4" ED Add) |==>| L x W x H / 139 DIM Weight| | Perimeter Buffer Zone | | C-Flute (+3/8" ED Add) | | ISTA 1A Prototype Test | +-----------------------+ +---------------------------+ +---------------------------+ | v [ ZERO-ERROR PACKAGING FULFILLMENT ] - 100% CAD Dieline Fitment - Zero Transit Product Damage - Lowest Volumetric Shipping Tier 1. Introduction Measuring custom boxes correctly is the systematic process of recording internal dimensions in the strict packaging industry sequence of Length $\times$ Width $\times$ Depth ($\text{L} \times \text{W} \times \text{D}$) based on the box opening facing upward. It is not a casual exercise with a flexible sewing tape measure; it is a foundational packaging engineering discipline. A miscalculated fraction of an inch will derail your entire production run, leaving you with thousands of unusable boxes, crushed products, or astronomical freight bills. THE HIGH COST OF DIMENSIONAL ERRORS UN-CALIBRATED MEASUREMENT METRICS ENGINEERED CAD BOX MEASUREMENT +-----------------------------------+ +-----------------------------------+ | Product Shifting & Seam Rupture | | Precision Snug Product Lock-In | | 11% Average Transit Damage Rates | VS | Zero Product Transit Breakage | | Heavy Carrier DIM Freight Penalty | | Optimized Volumetric Freight Tier | | Wasted Void Fill & Material Cost | | Zero Waste / No Excess Void Fill | +-----------------------------------+ +-----------------------------------+ Relying on guesswork creates severe operational leakage across your supply chain. Industry logistics data confirms that approximately 11% of un-optimized e-commerce parcels arrive damaged —a metric driven heavily by improperly sized boxes that allow products to slam against outer walls or buckle under stacking loads. To avoid costly mistakes, every brand manager and operations lead must understand the cardinal rule of structural packaging: packaging manufacturers always build to Internal Dimensions (ID) to fit the product, whereas shipping carriers always bill based on External Dimensions (ED) . Failing to account for the thickness of the corrugated board itself means your product won't fit inside, or you'll pay carrier penalties for shipping empty air. This blueprint breaks down the exact science of custom box measurement. You will learn the industry-standard sequence, corrugated board flute thickness additions, CAD score-line offsets, dimensional weight (DIM) freight formulas, real-world brand benchmarks, and a 5-step framework to guarantee your custom boxes fit perfectly every time. 2. Core Baseline Headings The Golden Rule of Box Dimensions: Industry Sequence, Orientation, and Internal vs. External Metrics Before picking up a ruler or opening CAD software, you must lock down the orientation of the box. Misinterpreting which side represents Length versus Depth will produce a dieline that is completely flipped, resulting in a box that cannot be assembled or packed. THE MANDATORY INDUSTRY SEQUENCE TOP OPENING FACING UPWARD +-----------------------------------+ / /| / LENGTH (L) / | +-----------------------------------+ | | | | | | | WIDTH (W) DEPTH (D) | | / | |/ +-----------------------------------+ Length (L) = Longest side of the top opening. Width (W) = Shorter side of the top opening (perpendicular to Length). Depth (D) = Vertical distance from bottom inside floor to top opening score line. The Mandatory Industry Sequence ($\text{Length} \times \text{Width} \times \text{Depth}$) Packaging engineers, die-makers, and automated folding machines operate on a single, non-negotiable metric sequence: Length ($\text{L}$): The longest side of the box opening when looking directly down into the open container. Width ($\text{W}$): The shorter side of the box opening, positioned at a $90^\circ$ angle (perpendicular) to the Length. Depth / Height ($\text{D}$ or $\text{H}$): The vertical dimension measured from the inside bottom floor of the box up to the top opening score line. Orienting the Opening Correctly The opening axis dictates the entire measurement sequence. If you are designing a Roll End Tuck Top (RETT) mailer, the "top" is the large clamshell lid. If you are measuring a tall Reverse Tuck End (RTE) folding carton for a lotion bottle, the "opening" is still the top flap. Confusing Depth with Length reverses the structural blank on the printing press, ruining the layout and rendering the batch unusable. Internal Dimensions (ID) vs. External Dimensions (ED) Internal Dimensions (ID): The usable space inside the box. All custom packaging manufacturers require ID specs because structural CAD software calculates fold allowances from the inside out to ensure your product fits snugly. External Dimensions (ED): The total physical space the box occupies on the outside. Carriers, freight forwarders, and 3PL warehouses use ED specs to calculate dimensional weight billing and pallet racking density. Substrate Chemistry & Board Flute Allowances: How Material Thickness Alters Box Volume A box is not a paper-thin 2D square—it is a 3D structure made from material with real physical thickness. When corrugated board is creased and folded $90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$, the material takes up space. CAD software accounts for this through score allowances. CORRUGATED BOARD FLUTE PROFILE CALIPERS OUTER LINERBOARD =================== FLUTE MEDIUM /\ /\ /\ /\ /\ /\ <--- Structural fluting adds INNER LINERBOARD =================== physical wall thickness (E-Flute = 1/16" Wall | B-Flute = 1/8" Wall | C-Flute = 11/64" Wall | BC-Flute = 1/4" Wall) Corrugated Board Flute Thickness Calibrations To calculate the true External Dimensions (ED) from your target Internal Dimensions (ID), you must add the board's caliper expansion allowance across all three axes ($\text{L} \times \text{W} \times \text{D}$): E-Flute Micro-Corrugated ($1/16\text{ in}$ / $0.0625\text{ in}$ Wall Thickness): Adds approximately $+1/8\text{ in}$ ($0.125\text{ in}$) to internal dimensions to determine total outer dimensions. Ideal for sleek D2C mailer boxes ($0\text{--}10\text{ lbs}$). B-Flute Corrugated ($1/8\text{ in}$ / $0.125\text{ in}$ Wall Thickness): Adds approximately $+1/4\text{ in}$ ($0.25\text{ in}$) to external dimensions. Delivers drop-impact cushioning for medium parcel goods ($10\text{--}25\text{ lbs}$). C-Flute Corrugated ($11/64\text{ in}$ / $0.171\text{ in}$ Wall Thickness): Adds approximately $+3/8\text{ in}$ ($0.375\text{ in}$) to external measurements. The standard profile for heavy master shipping cases. Double-Wall BC-Flute ($1/4\text{ in}$ / $0.25\text{ in}$ Wall Thickness): Adds up to $+1/2\text{ in}$ ($0.50\text{ in}$) to outer measurements, engineered for industrial freight over $50\text{ lbs}$. INTERNAL TO EXTERNAL CONVERSION MATRIX BOARD GRADE FLUTE THICKNESS LENGTH / WIDTH ADDITION DEPTH / HEIGHT ADDITION +---------------+ +-----------------+ +------------------------+ +-----------------------+ | E-Flute | | 1/16" (0.0625") | | + 1/8" (0.125") | | + 1/8" (0.125") | | B-Flute | | 1/8" (0.1250") | | + 1/4" (0.250") | | + 1/4" (0.250") | | C-Flute | | 11/64"(0.1710") | | + 3/8" (0.375") | | + 3/8" (0.375") | | BC Double-Wall| | 1/4" (0.2500") | | + 1/2" (0.500") | | + 1/2" (0.500") | +---------------+ +-----------------+ +------------------------+ +-----------------------+ CAD Score Line Center-to-Center Deductions When a steel scoring rule presses into corrugated board during die-cutting, it creates a crease. Packaging CAD systems calculate fold allowances from the center-to-center of those score lines. If a designer ignores score allowances, the inner linerboard will compress and buckle during folding, causing corner seam tears and pushing the box's outer dimensions beyond allowable tolerances. Paperboard Caliper Measurements for Folding Cartons For primary retail boxes made from Solid Bleached Sulfate (SBS) or Coated Unbleached Kraft (CUK) paperboard, material thickness is measured in caliper points ( $1\text{ pt} = 0.001\text{ in}$ ). While an $18\text{pt}$ or $24\text{pt}$ paperboard adds less outer bulk than corrugated board, precise score allowances remain essential to ensure tuck flaps close smoothly without popping open on store shelves. 3. Comparison Section: Measuring Methods, Accuracy Levels, & Logistics Impact Matrix Logistics carriers calculate shipping costs based on Dimensional Weight (DIM Weight)—a volumetric pricing formula that charges for the physical space a package occupies inside a delivery truck: $$\text{Dimensional Weight (lbs)} = \frac{\text{Length (in)} \times \text{Width (in)} \times \text{Height (in)}}{139}$$ Failing to account for board thickness or leaving unmeasured gaps can inflate your box's outer footprint. An uncalibrated $0.5\text{-inch}$ error across all dimensions can easily push a parcel into a higher dimensional weight tier, driving up shipping costs across thousands of orders. Their structural design teams measure products down to fractional millimeter tolerances. By calculating precise air-displacement tolerances between the inner tray and outer telescoping lid, Apple creates a controlled two-second friction drop during unboxing. This eliminates internal product movement without requiring single-use plastic foam. APPLE TELESCOPING AIR-RELEASE MECHANICS +-------------------------------+ | RIGID OUTER LID | | +-------------------------+ | <=== Micronic air gap creates resistance | | INNER GREYBOARD TRAY | | | | | | <=== Smooth, controlled 2-second drop | | [ PRODUCT CENTERED ] | | | +-------------------------+ | +-------------------------------+ Glossier: Tailored RETT Mailer Sizing Glossier avoids generic stock shipping boxes by engineering custom E-flute Roll End Tuck Top (RETT) mailers sized to match specific product combinations. By right-sizing the internal volume, Glossier eliminates the need for loose fill peanuts or air pillows while keeping shipments in the lowest possible carrier dimensional weight tiers. Custom Fitment Pioneers: Molded Pulp & Corrugated Insert Alignment Leading consumer electronics and cosmetics brands measure primary containers with digital calipers to engineer custom die-cut corrugated or molded pulp inserts. These inserts lock items in the center of the box, maintaining a consistent $0.5\text{-inch}$ perimeter buffer zone that protects fragile components from external impacts during postal sorting. 5. The Deep-Dive Solution Section: 5-Step Action Framework — How to Measure Custom Boxes Correctly for Your Products Follow this step-by-step framework to accurately measure your product and convert those metrics into a production-ready CAD dieline. 5-STEP BOX MEASUREMENT WORKFLOW STEP 1: Orient the Product & Establish the Opening Axis [Place product in packing position, lock L x W x D axis facing upward] | v STEP 2: Take Precise Physical Bounds Measurements [Use steel rule or calipers, measure maximum L x W x D points] | v STEP 3: Add Clearance Tolerances & Perimeter Buffer Zones [Add 1/16" to 1/8" snug fit clearance + 0.5" for tissue/inserts] | v STEP 4: Factor in Board Flute Profiles to Calculate ED & DIM [Add flute caliper values (+1/8" to +3/8") to verify carrier DIM freight] | v STEP 5: Order an Unprinted Structural CAD Sample Prototype [Build 1-off white sample, test product fitment, run 3-foot ISTA drop test] Step 1: Orient the Product & Establish the Opening Axis Place your product (or complete multi-item kit) on a flat table in the exact position it will sit inside the open box. Identify the top opening axis facing upward. From this perspective, lock in your measurement axes: Length ($\text{L}$): The longest horizontal side. Width ($\text{W}$): The shorter horizontal side perpendicular to Length. Depth ($\text{D}$): The vertical distance from the table surface to the top of the product. PRODUCT ORIENTATION & AXIS LOCK +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ | LOOKING DOWN AT OPEN CONTAINER AXIS | | | | [ LENGTH (L): Longest horizontal edge ] | | [ WIDTH (W): Shorter horizontal edge ] | | [ DEPTH (D): Vertical height from table floor ] | +-----------------------------------------------------------------+ Step 2: Take Precise Physical Bounds Measurements Using a rigid steel rule or digital calipers, measure the maximum outer dimensions of your product. Always measure across the widest points, accounting for protruding caps, dropper tops, handles, or pumps. Never squeeze or compress flexible items during measurement. MEASURING PROTRUDING ACCENTS INCORRECT (MEASURING BOTTLE BODY ONLY) CORRECT (MEASURING MAXIMUM BOUNDS) +---------------------------------+ +---------------------------------+ | Ignores extended pump nozzle | | Includes pump nozzle tip | | Ignores wide base flange | VS | Includes widest bottle shoulder | | Result: Box lid crushes cap! | | Result: Perfect internal fit! | +---------------------------------+ +---------------------------------+ Step 3: Add Clearance Tolerances & Perimeter Buffer Zones A box built to the exact millimeter of a product will be too tight to pack easily. Add appropriate clearance allowances to your product measurements to establish your target Internal Dimensions (ID) : Standard Snug Fitment: Add $+1/16\text{ in}$ to $+1/8\text{ in}$ ($1.5\text{ mm}$ to $3\text{ mm}$) to Length, Width, and Depth. Wrapped Products (Tissue Paper / Bubble Wrap): Add $+1/4\text{ in}$ ($6\text{ mm}$) across all axes. Custom Die-Cut Inserts: If using foam, molded pulp, or corrugated partitions, include a $0.5\text{-inch}$ perimeter buffer zone between the insert frame and the outer box walls. Step 4: Factor in Board Flute Profiles to Calculate External Dimensions & Freight DIM Convert your target Internal Dimensions (ID) into External Dimensions (ED) by adding board flute thickness values: $$\text{External Length} = \text{Internal Length} + \text{Flute Allowance}$$ $$\text{External Width} = \text{Internal Width} + \text{Flute Allowance}$$ $$\text{External Depth} = \text{Internal Depth} + \text{Flute Allowance}$$ For example, if your internal target for a D2C mailer is $8 \times 5 \times 3\text{ inches}$ using E-flute board ($+1/8\text{ in}$ allowance), your external dimensions will be $8.125 \times 5.125 \times 3.125\text{ inches}$ . Use these external metrics in the carrier DIM formula ($\text{ED L} \times \text{ED W} \times \text{ED D} / 139$) to confirm your billable shipping weight. Step 5: Order an Unprinted Structural CAD Sample Prototype Never approve mass production based solely on digital files. Request a single unprinted white structural prototype (unprinted sample) from your packaging manufacturer. Complete a final pre-production check: Physical Fitment Test: Place the product inside to confirm it slides in smoothly and stays secure without bulging the box walls. Closure Mechanics Check: Verify that tuck flaps and lock tabs close securely with proper friction tension. ISTA 1A Drop Test: Pack the sample and perform a 3-foot drop test onto corners, edges, and flat surfaces to confirm the structure protects the product under impact. PRE-PRODUCTION CHECKLIST [ ] Physical Product Fitment & Clearance Test [ ] Tuck Flap Friction Lock Tension Verification [ ] Internal Dimension (ID) vs. External Dimension (ED) Audit [ ] Carrier DIM Weight Freight Calculation Check [ ] ISTA 1A Multi-Angle Drop Test (3-Foot Impact) 6. Conclusion Measuring custom boxes correctly requires strictly following the industry sequence of Length × Width × Depth ($\text{L} \times \text{W} \times \text{D}$) , accounting for internal clearances, calibrating corrugated flute thicknesses, and verifying fitment with physical structural prototypes. Double-checking your measurements from the inside out protects your product, prevents manufacturing delays, and lowers your overall landed shipping costs. Strategic Execution Rule: Always double-check your measurements from the inside out—never assume outer stock box dimensions equal usable inner space.
